#4757. 9 Best Cooling Sheets for More Comfortable Sleep, Tested by Editors

We tested dozens of cooling sheets. My Sheets Rock makes the best.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

I always thought cooling sheets were a marketing gimmick until I actually tried them while I was nine months pregnant—in the middle of July. It was the first time in months that I didn’t wake up with my sweaty hair matted against my head, and I’ve never looked back.

It’s important to get this out of the way now: Cooling sheets aren’t magic. They’re not going to keep you from sweating if you sleep under a heavy comforter or it’s warm in your bedroom at night. But they do cause a noticeable difference in how you feel between the sheets, and are one more element to help regulate your body temperature at night.

These are a few of our favorite sheet sets, but read on for more detailed reviews:

“The ideal temperature for sleeping is no cooler than 66 degrees and no warmer than 72 degrees,” says neuroscientist and sleep specialist Allison Brager, PhD. “This was study-approved, tested, and evaluated by some NASA scientists.” Resting in this temperate climate can support better sleep and, ultimately, improved health. Regularly shortchanging your sleep leads to a higher risk of obesity, depression, and type 2 diabetes, along with other health issues. But having good, consistent sleep can do the opposite.

That’s why, even though cooling sheets are usually more expensive than regular sheets, they’re a worthwhile investment that will help support more restorative sleep, Brager says, and, as a result, improve your overall quality of life.

So, how can you tell which bedding option will help you hit that not-so-hot spot? Cooling sheets—especially those made from fabrics like microfiber, linen, and bamboo—can help keep your body at the right temp for restful sleep. The best cooling sheets can help reduce heat buildup and manage moisture, but your comfort also depends on your room and bedding.

The Regulator sheets are made from rayon derived from bamboo and felt lightweight, silky, and cool to the touch, according to our testers.

“They’re very soft, and I’m able to wake up not sweaty,” says Women’s Health digital designer Taryn Colbert, who has zero complaints about these sheets.

WH contributor and self-professed "hot sleeper" Lily Wohlner is also a fan. She had never owned a set of cooling sheets, but quickly fell in love with these. They're "super thin, which automatically makes them nice and light,” Wohlner says. “But they're also temperature-regulating and moisture-wicking, so you stay fresh and cool while you snooze.” She also loves how silky smooth they feel against the skin without that "crunchy" feeling found in lesser, lower-quality sheets.

There is one catch to the ultra-lightweight design, however. "Due to their weight, I find that these sheets tend to bunch up at the bottom of my bed, which I don't love," Wohlner says. "Every time I go to make my bed, I have to fish under my comforter to find them, which adds time to the already dreaded process." (Colbert hasn’t experienced this.)

It's not a deal-breaker for us, but something to be aware of. Plus, we found that the natural stretch of these sheets means making (or re-making) the bed is a snap.

Bamboo is often touted as more eco-friendly because it's possible to harvest more per acre than cotton and is typically grown without pesticides. However, the experts we spoke with warned that the raw material goes through serious chemical refinement before it's turned into bedding.

Overall, our team loved these sheets for their buttery soft, featherweight design and the ability to keep us cool and sweat-free even on the hottest summer nights. They're a great midrange set that we recommend for anyone looking to level up from the cheapest available options (like Mellanni's four-piece Iconic Sheet Set), but who isn't quite ready to splurge on an ultra-luxe set.

“Jill of all trades; master of none.” That's the perfect way to describe Mellanni's Iconic Collection, including the four-piece set of cooling sheets we tested for this year's roundup. These sheets aren't the softest, the most luxurious, or the absolute best at cooling. But they are a solid all-around buy that feels better, looks better, and cools better than most other sets that cost three times as much.

"My girlfriend and I have slept on these for the last month, and we've been pleasantly surprised by how good they feel for the price," Richard says. "They feel much better and cozier against the skin than most other sheets I've tested in this price range."

Fellow tester and self-described hot sleeper Janie Booth, associate video producer at WH, also praises the feel of these sheets. “They are very soft,” she says.

The synthetic microfiber construction in this sheet set isn't purposely designed for cooling. In fact, the weave is tighter than other sheets made with natural fibers. But the material is thin enough to be surprisingly breathable, without feeling threadbare. "I actually took these glamping on a long, hot, late June weekend," Richard says. "For sticky, sweaty nights, the thickness of these sheets was perfect, and I found them much more breathable than most microfiber sheets."

On the downside, that same microfiber—polyester, really—construction means these aren't as absorbent or moisture-wicking as natural alternatives either. So, they're not as good at whisking away sweat to help further cool your body.

Like most microfiber fabrics, these sheets are surprisingly durable, though, thanks to the previously mentioned tight weave. We've found they hold up well, even after repeated washings with no loose threads, shedding, or fading. (Booth noticed some pilling, but Richard didn’t.) Plus, they're more wrinkle-resistant than most.

The biggest thing these cooling sheets have going for them is price. They're significantly cheaper (in some cases, by more than 75 percent) than every other set in this year's roundup. Plus, with Amazon's generous free shipping and free returns policy, it's almost like you're getting a legit in-home sleep trial.

One additional bonus is that these sheets are available in a much wider selection of colors and patterns than any other we tested. That's especially nice if you're keen to match the look of your new cooling sheets to the rest of your bedroom decor.

There are a lot of high-tech fabric blends out there designed to keep you cool, but classic cotton sheets can still work wonders. Brooklinen’s Classic Percale Core Sheet Set is a favorite in my household—so much so that I’ll try to wash them quickly when I do laundry to get them back on my mattress before I need to swap in a different set. These were the sheets I splurged on when I was heavily pregnant and hot. They still feel luxurious and crisp, even though I’ve had them in heavy rotation for two years.

The sheets are made with percale cotton, which means it’s woven into a grid pattern to give it a crisp, cool feel. It’s almost like a dress shirt, but softer, and with a noticeable coolness when you slide between the sheets.

Christian Gollayan, style and reviews director at Men's Health and Women's Health, is also a fan. “I’m a hot sleeper and usually need my bedroom below 69 degrees to avoid getting sweaty,” he says. “These kept me comfortable through fall, winter, and spring.”

Gollayan says his sheets held up “remarkably well” for nearly two years with weekly washings. When he did sweat in deep summer, Gollayan says his sheets didn’t hold onto an odor the way some other sets he’s tried have. The sheets have thoughtful details that I love, too, like envelope closures to keep your pillows from sliding out and tags that designate which end of the fitted sheet is the long and short side.

While Gollayan and I both enjoy these sheets, he noticed some fraying in his set after two years. (I haven’t had the same experience, although the rich blue color in my tandem stripes is fading.) They also felt a little stiff at first, but quickly soften up with time and repeat washings. They’re not the cheapest cooling sheets you’ll find, but they’re pretty durable and luxe.

Casper is perhaps best known for its excellent cooling mattresses. But you might be surprised to learn the company also makes great cooling bedding. After testing over a dozen cooling sheets, Casper's Hyperlite Sheet Set earned our 'Best Runner-Up' spot for its soft, ultra-lightweight feel, the fact it looks more premium than its price should allow, and, most importantly, its 100 percent Tencel Lyocell construction. The fabric excels at fighting sweat and overheating, thanks to its structure, which absorbs and releases moisture while promoting good airflow.

“They're definitely cooling without being too ‘cold,’” says WH digital designer and tester Leeann Mattern. Fellow tester Mike Richard also praises the sheets’ lightweight, cooling feel, which he says is great year-round. But, in warmer weather, he says they do an excellent job at regulating temperature and wicking away sweat and moisture. That's thanks in large part to the tencel lyocell material and the unique, vented grid-weave pattern that Casper uses to help promote better airflow while you sleep. Bonus: Our team loved that same grid pattern elevates the vibe of these sheets above the traditional (and often boring) flat aesthetic of most sheets with a lightly textured look and feel.

We're hard-pressed to find much to complain about with these cooling sheets, but there are a few minor concerns to keep in mind. "My only gripe is that I wish they were a little softer because they're not quite as buttery or luxurious as the true bamboo and bamboo blend options we tested," Richard says. That's largely due to their lower 200-thread-count construction (incidentally, that was the lowest of any sheets we tested this year). "I did find that they soften after a few washes, however, and hold up well to repeated machine-washings, too."

Mattern also says the lightweight fabric allows patterns in her mattress and pillow to show through, so that’s something to be aware of if you’re especially concerned about aesthetics. On that note, our team of sleep testers were a bit bummed by the lack of available color options—this sheet set only comes in white.

We would also love it if Casper expanded its return policy beyond the lackluster 30 days. That's surprisingly thin compared to the competition, and the sheets must be returned in their original, unused condition, which doesn't allow for a true "sleep trial."

Of course, you don't have to spend hundreds to score a decent set of cooling sheets. But, sometimes, you really do get what you pay for. That's true of Bedgear's Ver-Tex Sheet Set. They're pricier than most we tested this year, but oh so worth it with a performance-minded design that keeps you cool and stays put, even during your most "vigorous" bed activities.

The Ver-Tex Sheet Set is the only one in this year's roundup made of 100 percent nylon. Like many synthetic materials, nylon isn't typically absorbent or very good at wicking away moisture. "I initially planned to test these out in my guest room," Richard says. "But my girlfriend and I loved how cool-to-the-touch they were, and found them way softer and airier than we expected, so we wound up putting them on our bed."

The nylon is extremely breathable, allowing them to cool better than most. In very humid environments (think Miami in August), however, we did notice that they felt slightly clammier than other natural fabric sets our team tested. “This is such a ridiculous thing to say, but they almost did their job too well,” says fellow tester and WH social media editor Alyssa Cruz. “I sometimes wake up cold and need to add extra blankets.” Because of this, she plans to switch them out during the chillier winter months.

Still, our team agrees that these sheets are worth the $300 price tag. “I love the feeling the most,” Cruz says. “These are the softest sheets I have ever felt, and almost feel like activewear. They make falling asleep feel luxurious.”

Plus, one of this set's biggest selling points is its ability to stretch and provide an extremely good fit, thanks to Bedgear's unique Powerband. It's a thick, full-band elastic designed to grip the bottom of your mattress so it won't slip. The pillowcases included with the Ver-Tex sets also feature this same band, so we never wound up with our pillows inching their way out of the case. Everything stays put, so you're not left remaking the bed every night before tucking in.

There's almost nothing we dislike about these best-in-class cooling sheets. But we do wish they were available in more than four colors. They're also not sold in smaller sizes like Twin, Twin XL, or Full, which may or may not be a deal-breaker for you.

Lastly, these are among the priciest cooling sheets we tested over the past year. Still, we think you get what you pay for with this set. They're extremely durable, cool better than almost every other set we tested, and the ultra-snug fit for both the sheets and pillowcases is second to none.

PeachSkinSheets’ Classic Collection has a brushed polyester fabric that our testers found super soft. Somehow PeachSkinSheets manages to thread that needle (pun intended) with its Classic Collection. With an airy, breathable, smart poly-fiber construction, these sheets are surprisingly effective at keeping you cool, calm, and collected.

"I tested these in our guest suite, and the in-laws (self-described 'fussy' sleepers) and I both agreed that these do an incredible job at keeping you cool during the night," Richard says. "They feel more premium, more luxurious than the price tag would suggest." But more importantly, our entire test staff found these kept us cool while also doing a reasonable job of managing sweat and moisture. The athletic-grade construction is lighter than traditional cotton, and they breathe more like high-end (think Lululemon) athleisure apparel.

The sheets are OEKO-TEX STANDARD 100 certified, meaning they have been tested against limits for harmful substances. "My girlfriend has extremely sensitive skin, and even basic synthetics like polyester don't always agree with her, sometimes causing rashes and irritation," Richard says. "We were initially skeptical about these poly-fiber sheets, but she's had zero issues and finds them extremely comfortable."

The feel of these sheets was also a perk for WH associate style and reviews editor Shannen Zitz. “The sheets are super soft and smooth without causing me to overheat at night,” she says.

Zitz praises the deep corners of the fitted sheet, too. “I love that the fitted sheet actually stays on my bed,” she says. “My biggest issue with sheets is when they slip off the corners after just a few nights, but these have really deep corners so they stay put really well.” Every set also includes an extender panel, allowing the sheets to fit extra-deep (up to 22-inch) mattresses which covers just about every model on the market.

Unlike most of the competition, they're available in more than 30 colorways—everything from basic white and navy to bolder options like gold and neon orange—making it easy to match the aesthetic of your current bedroom setup.

After several months of testing, we found the Classic Collection cooling sheets to be extremely durable. "Even after repeated machine-washing and with two cats in my house, these sheets have stood up to teeth, claws, pills, pulls, and fading," Richard says. "Plus, fresh out of the wash, the wrinkles release almost instantly after making the bed, so I never have to worry about ironing them." The only gripe, per Zitz, is that the top sheet felt a little short. “I toss and turn a lot and, after a night or two, I find the bottom of the sheet comes untucked pretty easily,” she says. “If you like your sheets to feel really snug, it requires re-tucking.”

PeachSkinSheets also shines with a solid, 30-day return policy. Like SlumberCloud, it's more like an in-home sleep trial. Even opened bedding can be returned within 30 days for a full refund, so it's truly risk-free to try them out at home.

Most cooling bedding products are designed to draw away and evaporate moisture. But that means they only start working after you're already sweating and are probably miserable. Slumber Cloud's Performance Sheets take a different tack with a uniquely blended construction that actively regulates temperature the entire time you're sleeping to (ideally) keep you cool and comfortable before sweat ever becomes an issue.

The secret sauce to Slumber Cloud's Performance Sheets is a blend of reactive Tencel with Outlast viscose. Tencel is already one of our favorite fibers for cooling sheets, but the addition of Outlast levels up the entire setup. "I've used Outlast-infused hiking apparel before, and it's incredibly effective at regulating body temperature in hot or cold environments," Richard says. "The addition of Outlast in these sheets delivers best-in-class moisture-wicking, which is a game-changer if you're a hot (and potentially clammy) sleeper." The 300-thread-count material might appear to be lower quality than higher-end 500-plus-thread-count alternatives. But, these feel every bit softer than many premium sheets we've previously tested.

These sheets are soft to the touch, according to fellow tester and WH entertainment editor Amy Wilkinson. “But my absolute favorite thing about these sheets, which I've never encountered with another set, is the additional elastic band at the corners of the fitted sheet that help it wrap around virtually any size mattress you can imagine,” she says. Compared to the traditional "corner-sewn" elastics found in most traditional fitted sheets, the bands in this sheet set help keep it firmly in place.

One especially nice feature of all of Slumber Cloud's bedding: it offers a 30-night trial for purchases made directly from the brand.

If you’re an extra-hot sleeper, however, you may want to look elsewhere. While Wilkinson found these sheets cooling, she says that, despite claims about being designed with “NASA cooling technology,” they didn’t seem to cool her off better than her previous sheet set. Still, they are great at wicking moisture and are incredibly durable.

(Pro tip: The Performance Sheet Set is, in our opinion, Slumber Cloud's best cooling sheet set. But, if you're looking for almost-as-good performance with a classic sheet feel, opt for its Essential Sheet Set which blends cotton with Outlast fibers.)

If you love the silky smoothness of cotton sateen sheets, Sijo’s AiryWeight Eucalyptus Sheets offer a similar feel while being 70 percent more moisture-absorbing. Made with naturally hypoallergenic Tencel Lyocell, the glossy silk-like texture of the sheets is a great option for those with sensitive skin, especially if certain materials make you feel itchy. Plus, the set boasts OEKO-TEX and Asthma and Allergy Friendly certifications.

“The feel of these are incredible,” says WH fitness editor Cori Ritchey. “With cooling sheets, I tend to fear they're going to be too slick and not cozy. These are kind of the perfect blend.” The sheets feel silky but not slippery, she adds.

At $185 for a queen-size set, these Sijo sheets aren’t cheap, but they are long lasting. The brand claims the sheets survived 2,000 rubs without pilling in lab testing. They passed Ritchey’s personal durability test, too: “They wash very nicely—they don't seem to lose their texture the longer you use them,” she says. And for those of us whose top sheet ends up on the floor most nights, you can subtract the flat sheet from the set for a $75 discount.

One of the downsides of the sheets is the two-month return window that only applies if the bedding is unopened—but there is a catch here. Sijo offers a 30-night bedding trial for eligible direct purchases. Return-shipping charges depend on whether you purchased Checkout+, so check the terms before ordering. Some customers have also noted that the sheets shrink a little after the first wash (we didn’t notice this during testing, but it’s worth flagging).

Some hot sleepers merely need sheets that are breathable throughout the night, while others prefer bedding that is immediately cool to the touch. If you want a set of sheets that feels like sleeping on the cool side of the pillow all night long, Sijo’s AiryWeight Eucalyptus Sheets are for you. “I'm normally a hot sleeper and these have kept me cool and comfortable,” Ritchey says.

Linen sheets are a great option for hot sleepers, if you’re willing to spend a little more. Brooklinen’s Linen Core Sheets are made with 100 percent European flax that softens with each wash, although they may be a little rough for sensitive skin right out of the box. The sheets are breathable yet they have a weight to them, which makes them great for year-round use.

“These sheets are so soft and cozy—truly the most comfortable material I have ever slept on,” says WH associate editor Olivia Luppino. “I actively look forward to getting into bed with them.” She describes the sheets as plush to the touch, while still maintaining a sleekness that gives them a cooling feel. “They definitely keep me cool in warm summer months,” she says. “I’m very into these sheets.”

That said, one of the (few) downsides is the $300-plus price tag, which is expensive but not outrageous when it comes to linen sheets. Plus, Brooklinen tends to run frequent sales, so it’s not unusual to see a 25 percent discount. The sheets have gotten softer with each wash, but at the same time they wear like iron with no snagging, pulling, or pilling to be found.

They are also OEKO-TEX certified and come with the longest return window of our favorite cooling sheets at a whopping 365 days. If you’re looking to make an investment that will last and keep you cool in any climate, Brooklinen’s Linen Core Sheets are worth the splurge.

To curate a list of the best cooling sheets, we recruited eight Women's Health staffers to personally vet a wide range of sets in various temperatures and environments over the past year. For instance, we slept in Casper's Hyperlite Sheet Set in July with no air-conditioning, glamped with Mellanni's Iconic Collection in New Hampshire, and cozied up in SlumberCloud's Performance Sheet Set with the window open in 80-degree heat “for science.” Then, our testing editors narrowed the selections by evaluating each sheet set based on style, fit, price point, comfort, breathability, moisture management, softness, durability after washing, wrinkling or pilling, and value.

It probably goes without saying that sheet material matters above all else. Natural fibers, like linen and cotton, are often best, according to Brager. They tend to be more breathable and absorbent (more on why that's actually a good thing below) than others, which means they won't trap heat that can make you sweat as you catch your Z's.

Your sheets’ weave is the pattern used to hold the threads together to make the fabric. Percale is generally considered the best weave for hot sleepers. This type of weave uses a simple pattern that maximizes airflow and has a lightweight feel, lowering the odds it will trap body heat while you snooze.

It’s generally recommended that you avoid sateen or flannel sheets if you’re looking for a cooling feel. These tend to be denser and hold onto heat as a result.

There are so many factors that go into how cool you feel when you slip between the sheets at night, including the temperature of your room, your body temperature, the weight of your comforter, and your mattress composition. But we sweat a lot throughout the night. "If you don't have something that's absorbent, you will marinate in sweat," Young says. That's why natural materials that are highly absorbent, like linen and cotton, are important. "Even more important than that is wicking, which means getting moisture to the surface for evaporation," says Young. The two of these features working in tandem is what keeps you both dry and cool.

Moisture-wicking sheets can be one element to help keep you cool at night. These sheets are specially designed to pull moisture away from your skin and evaporate, allowing you to feel cooler, faster. They also tend to feel a little airier than other sheets.

That doesn’t mean you won’t ever feel hot if you use moisture-wicking sheets—again, there’s a lot happening when you sleep that can influence your body’s temperature. But you can usually feel a difference between how you feel when using moisture-wicking sheets and other types of sheets.

Beyond the material of your cooling sheets, the quality of that material is important. Back in the day, thread count was the single most important measure of quality in bedding. Anything above 600-thread-count was often considered good, while 800 and above was downright luxurious. But advances in technology have allowed us to create sheets with a 1,500, even 2,000, thread count. That’s not necessarily a good thing, as that figure can be inflated and used as a marketing gimmick.

Plus, super-high thread-count sheets usually aren’t all they're cracked up to be. “My experience with those is that they’re not strong, and they don’t hold up well,” says Deborah Young, owner of TheTextileExpert.com and a clinical assistant professor of textiles at Arizona State University. “They are seductively soft, but for me, there’s a point of diminishing returns.”

Thread count can be a measure of quality, but you'll want to consider other factors, too, especially when shopping for the best cooling sheets. Some manufacturers rely on GSM (or grams per square meter) as this is a measure of weight rather than thread density.

Young's most important tip for hot sleepers, however, is that they may actually benefit from sheets with a lower thread count (like 400). A higher thread count often means the sheets are denser, offering better coverage, but a hot sleeper would probably want to avoid this.

It depends. Every brand we recommend below offers a return policy with a minimum 30-day term. Some, however, only accept returns for unopened sheet sets in the original packaging. Others provide longer terms (up to 365 days) with no questions asked, effectively like a free in-home trial.

There are a variety of certifications out there to ensure that consumers are getting high-quality bedding and textiles. One of the most common labels you’ll find on sheets is the OEKO-TEX Standard 100 certification, which means that the product has been tested for more than 1,000 harmful substances. Some sheets may also have sustainability labels, like FSC certification, or an Asthma & Allergy Friendly certification from the Asthma and Allergy Foundation of America. Keep in mind that more certifications tend to lead to a higher price tag, though—and not all are necessary.

Our favorite cooling sheets range in price from $37 to $322 for a queen-size set. There’s no need to spend hundreds on a set of sheets—you can easily find high-quality cooling sheets for $100-plus. However, certain fabrics like linen will cost more and in return should survive many years of use.

Women’s Health first wrote this story in 2019 and has been continuously testing new cooling sheets as they’re released. During that time, some clear favorites have emerged. For this update, we had several WH staffers and contributors test these products in their own beds. Each sheet set was tested for two to three weeks or longer, and evaluated on their cooling abilities, softness, and durability, among other factors. Testers ranged from those who regularly wake up sweaty to people who consider themselves “neutral” in terms of sleep temperature.

Yes, cooling sheets actually work. They’re designed to be lightweight, breathable, and moisture-wicking, all of which can make you feel cooler when you sleep at night. However, there are a lot of factors that influence how hot you feel at night, including the type of mattress and comforter you have. Ultimately, cooling sheets are one more way to help you feel comfortable, but they shouldn’t be the only thing you use if you tend to run hot while you sleep.

Cotton is usually considered best, but you have a few options to choose from when it comes to cooling materials for sheets.

Bamboo sheets can be cooler than cotton sheets, but that’s not always the case. The weave of your sheets matters. A cotton percale weave sheet can be very cooling and even more cooling than standard bamboo sheets. But cotton is also used to make flannel sheets—which are heat-insulating, not cooling—making it hard to rely on fabric alone when choosing the best cooling sheets.

Thread count is usually linked to the softness of sheets, but it can impact how cool sheets feel. A higher thread count typically means that sheets are denser, which can work against your efforts to stay cool. That’s why Young suggests choosing sheets with a lower thread count, like 400, over much higher thread count options.

Cooling sheets should be washed as often as “regular” sheets, which means they should be washed every week, says Kelly Murray, a certified pediatric and adult sleep coach in Chicago. This will allow you to wash away any allergens, keeping your sheets feeling crisp and fresh, she adds.

By the way, you should wash your cooling sheets before using them, too. "You're washing off any dust the sheets may have collected in the warehouse, which can irritate your respiratory system and lead to sleep issues,” Murray says.

Some cooling sheets, especially those made with natural fibers like cotton and linen, soften with each successive wash. If your new set feels a little too stiff or "crunchy," try running them through a machine wash cycle or two to soften them.

There is an almost universal rule among experts that you should be changing your sheets every week, and Murray concurs. If you don't want to wash your sheets that often, you should consider purchasing an extra set to swap out each week.

As for when it's time to swap out cooling sheets for brand new ones, that's up to you. Murray says she purchases a new set whenever she sees them on sale, but recommends replacing yours about every two to three years.

ICYDK, your body temperature needs to drop about 2 degrees lower at night in order to synthesize melatonin, Murray says. So, it is super important that you create an environment that allows for this. That means ensuring your bedroom is "dark, cool, and quiet" when you're ready for bed.

Other than investing in some cooling sheets, you can also improve your sleep quality by keeping a consistent sleep routine that involves ending screen time at least an hour before you go to bed. "Your body and brain are always looking for patterns throughout the day to know what happens next," Murray says. "So if you have a consistent bedtime routine that's very relaxing, that will trigger the production of melatonin and help your brain to unwind."

#4755. This Designer Finds Unexpected Beauty in Marble’s Leftovers

Wandering through the ruins of Pompeii, the ancient Roman city frozen in time by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius, one is struck by that civilization’s devotion to precious materials. Surviving mosaics depict the opulence that once filled the city’s lavish homes. These fragments of classical life, and the richness with which they were rendered, captured the imagination of Polish-born designer Daniel Kolodziejczak, inspiring his upcoming Tesserae series for the New York design gallery Ateliers Courbet.

A vessel in rock crystal, smoky quartz, and citrine quartz

Sun hits a pendant in rock crystal and smoky quartz.

Kolodziejczak creates objects in marble, precious stones, and bronze at his workshop in Carrara, Italy.

Kolodziejczak, who started as a jewelry designer in Paris for brands like Givenchy and Saint Laurent, began making decorative objects and furniture after a move to Milan. His exhibition at Ateliers Courbet (on view until January 16, 2027) was inspired by fragments of leftover stone he found in the marble yards of Carrara, not far from his workshop. “Every time I go there I find myself buying new stones,” Kolodziejczak says.

Kolodziejczak with two vessels from his Tesserae series

A vessel in rock crystal, smoky quartz, and citrine quartz

The designer polishes the base to a console from his Tesserae series.

The remnants accumulated in his studio until, on a visit to Pompeii, he had “the idea to bring them together” in one exhibition. His vessel shapes, inspired by antique Roman pottery, are hand-carved in marble, along with materials like rock crystal, smoky quartz, and citrine quartz. The series will also include a monumental crystal pendant light, sconces in bronze with citrine quartz shades, a mirror, and massive stone tables. But despite the expansive scale, Kolodziejczak’s sensibility remains rooted in the concept of adornment. “I treat furniture like jewelry,” says the designer, whose Studio Daniel K is based in Milan and Paris. “These pieces aren’t meant to take up the entire room—just to be that accent of something extraordinary.”

#4754. Hormone Therapy May Boost Weight Loss on Wegovy, But Not as Much on Zepbound

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Females using menopause hormone therapy (MHT) alongside GLP-1 medications such as Ozempic or Wegovy may experience greater weight loss, according to a study presented at the 2026 Annual Meeting of the Menopause Society.

Weight gain is a common concern among middle-aged women. While much of this is associated with aging, hormonal changes during menopause can also contribute to changes in body fat and its distribution.

GLP-1 medications have been shown to be effective for weight loss. However, the results may vary by sex and reproductive stage.

For example, studies have found that women and adults under age 55 may experience greater weight loss with these medications.

A previous small observational study in postmenopausal women found that using MHT alongside semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy, was associated with greater weight loss.

However, whether hormone therapy influences weight loss outcomes with different GLP-1 medications remains unclear.

To investigate this question, researchers compared weight loss in middle-aged women receiving either semaglutide or tirzepatide, with or without MHT. The findings have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

The study included 3,855 women with an average age of 57 and an average body mass index (BMI) of 36 kg/m2.

The semaglutide cohort included 2,379 individuals, while the tirzepatide cohort included 1,476 individuals.

The average follow-up in the semaglutide cohort, both with and without MHT, was 26 months. The average follow-up in the tirzepatide group was 17 months for those using MHT and 16 months for those not using it.

The researchers found that in the semaglutide cohort, those using MHT alongside the GLP-1 medication had significantly greater weight loss at 9 months than those not using MHT.

These differences were sustained at 12 and 15 months and at the final follow-up. Those using MHT were also more likely to reach up to a 30% total body weight loss than those not using it.

In the tirzepatide cohort, those using MHT had a modestly greater weight loss at 3 months and were more likely to achieve more than 5% total body weight loss by the final follow-up. However, no significant difference in weight loss was observed at later time points.

These findings suggest that MHT use may be associated with greater weight loss among middle-aged women taking semaglutide. However, the researchers did not observe a sustained, statistically significant difference in weight loss among those taking tirzepatide.

Betul Hatipoglu, MD, Director of the Diabetes and Obesity Center at the University Hospitals Cleveland Medical Center, who was not involved in the study, told Healthline that the findings are encouraging.

However, she also cautioned that people should be careful not to interpret them as evidence that hormone therapy should be added to GLP-1 treatment specifically to enhance weight loss.

“This is an association, and the study provides an opportunity to discuss how menopause, aging, changes in body composition, and metabolic health can be present,” she said.

It is important to keep in mind that the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved certain hormone therapy medications to treat menopause symptoms such as hot flashes, night sweats, and vaginal dryness. However, these medications are not FDA-approved for weight loss or obesity management.

The study authors noted that larger studies are needed to confirm their observations and to inform individualized strategies for middle-aged females.

Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB-GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who was not involved in the study, noted that weight gain is one of the most common concerns she hears from women during menopause. Beyond affecting self-esteem and quality of life, excess abdominal fat can increase the risk of type 2 diabetes and heart disease.

“Finding effective, sustainable ways to manage weight is important for women’s long-term health and healthy aging,” she said.

“I would like to see prospective, randomized studies examining GLP-1 medications with and without hormone therapy to determine whether hormone therapy directly improves weight loss and helps women maintain it over time. In the meantime, treatment decisions should be individualized and guided by a healthcare professional.”

Ross advised that the decision should be based on your individual symptoms, health history, and treatment goals.

“Hormone therapy can significantly improve disruptive menopausal symptoms, including hot flashes, sleep disturbances, and mood changes. By helping women feel better and more energetic, it may also make it easier to exercise and manage their weight,” she said.

Hatipoglu noted that GLP-1-based medications, on the other hand, are effective treatments for obesity and can improve important aspects of metabolic health. Their use should be based on an individual’s weight-related health risks, medical history, and treatment goals.

“For a woman who has both bothersome menopausal symptoms and obesity, it may be entirely appropriate to consider both treatments. But I would not recommend starting hormone therapy solely to improve the weight-loss response to a GLP-1 medication based on the evidence currently available,” she said.

“It is also important to remember that successful weight management during and after menopause is about more than the number on the scale. Preserving muscle mass, maintaining bone health, improving metabolic health, and supporting long-term physical function are equally important.”

You should speak with your healthcare professional about the risks and benefits of all treatment options.

#4751. 23 Christmas Decoration Ideas, From Traditional Tartans to a Jewel-Toned Winter Wonderland

“Seeing holiday decor get a modern-design makeover is my Roman Empire,” says home expert Julian Thomas. These Christmas decoration ideas will set a festive tone in any room of the house—and yes, it’s possible to deck your halls in an elevated way. “In the past, if you decorated for the holidays you had to sacrifice style and aesthetics for nostalgia and Christmas necessities,” he says. “Not any more. From silk tree skirts to Clivia marble stocking holders, Christmas decorations have never been chicer.”

But if you’re more of a traditionalist, you’ll find inspiration to fit your style here, too. In fact, multiple design pros we spoke to mentioned that this year’s big trend is nostalgia (more on that below). With retro inspiration as well as new takes on festive color palettes, plus creative Christmas garlands and interior design-friendly stockings, here are 23 Christmas decor ideas for all kinds of merrymakers.

A dark and moody space shouldn’t stop you from merry decor for the holiday season—lean into it with your Christmas decorations.

“Red and green are traditional Christmas colors, but I love to break away from tradition a bit and use bright jewel tones to create a dramatic and sophisticated look for the holiday season,” says Annie Sloan, paint and color expert and creator of Chalk Paint. She is a fan of purple—once reserved for kings and emperors—for the holidays. “My Tyrian Plum Wall Paint is a rich, jewel-toned plum with maroon and red elements,” she says. “It works beautifully with metallics, fairy lights, and flickering candlelight to create a Christmas fit for the three kings!”

Glass jars of gelt and dreidels set a stylish holiday vignette.

For an easy DIY project, fill glass jars with small holiday decor items, like dreidels or gold coins, as seen in this Hanukkah-adorned living room arranged by LA-based designer Ethan Charles Greenfeld of Ethan Charles Design. Pinecones, tiny Christmas ornaments, bows, or mini Santa figures would all make great options as well.

Centering your tree in the entryway sets a festive tone right away.

Get more bang for your balsam by placing it in a spot in your living room that’s visible from other areas of the house—even better if you can see it from your home’s entryway. “I love making an impact with my tree and recommend putting it front and center if you can,” says designer Lauren Ashley of Lauren Ashley Experiences in Houston. “The tree is only up for a few weeks, so why not showcase it right at your entrance if there’s room?” Not only will guests get a peek at all your trimmings, you can enjoy the tree each time you come and go from your home.

Carry Christmas cheer throughout the house with wreaths and bows.

“I like to decorate the rooms we spend the most time in since Christmas decor just makes me so happy,” says lifestyle blogger and content creator Miyaeva Renae. “This year, I’m planning to decorate our living room, kitchen, bedroom, nursery, and even the bathrooms to bring that festive feeling throughout the house.” Here, Renae has wrapped kitchen cabinets in bows and placed mini wreaths on the backs of island chairs. Other small touches—like a wreath on the range hood, ribbon tied around a utensils jar, and a bowl filled with pinecones—add even more holiday cheer.

For those who leave gifts under the tree for a little while before Christmas day, it’s worth considering how the paper fits in with your decorative scheme.

This will inspire you to get your wrapping done early, and it gives your gift boxes another purpose: dressing up your living room before the big exchange on Christmas morning. “I love to make my own gift wrap,” Sloan says. “Buy cheap brown packing paper and paint it yourself with stripes, spots, or any design you fancy. Add contrasting ribbons and pile your gifts under the tree. Your gifts become part of your Christmas scheme. It’s stunning.” By making your own wrapping paper, you can also make sure it perfectly complements the rest of your decor.

Holiday-themed decals are a good—and renter-friendly—way to get your space looking festive.

For big impact without big effort, consider a high-quality wall sticker like the Victorian-inspired Christmas variety from Wallpick. “No tools are needed to apply Wallpick’s stickers, however I do recommend applying them to smooth walls for the best results,” says Wallpick’s founder Dina Jasmin. Use a wall sticker to frame your Christmas tree. Or, if a tree isn’t in the plans, the sticker can serve as a focal point and place to gather presents.

A Christmas tree, garland, wreath, and throw pillows add some Christmas cheer to this otherwise calm, neutral bedroom.

Wake up in a winter wonderland by hanging a wreath above the bed and wrapping bed posts in a garland and string lights. Throw pillows featuring trees or snowflakes add a further festive touch—and if you really want to go all out, put a pre-lit Christmas tree in your bedroom as well. This year, Renae is even extending the Christmas home decor beyond the primary suite: “I usually don’t decorate our guest bedroom, but since we’ll have family staying with us this, I’m planning to add some holiday touches there too along with all of the bathrooms,” she says. “It’s such a fun way to make every space feel festive and welcoming.”

What’s better than one Christmas tree in your entryway? Two.

“I love to host, so it’s not uncommon for friends and family to gather at my house throughout the season,” says Wendy Lau, Yale Home’s interior design consultant. While living rooms and dining areas may pull focus when it comes to Christmas decoration ideas, Lau greets guests with yuletide flair upon arrival: “One of my favorite places to decorate for the holidays is the entryway.” She uses a smart lock programmed with custom codes to help guests feel right at home, so they can see themselves in and be dazzled by eye-catching visuals like “greenery and twinkle lights—always a charming sight. I also like to drape garlands over the doorway and hang big wreaths with a jolly red bow out front.” A holiday-themed doormat at the front door as part of the porch decor completes the festive first impression.

This felt ball garland is a creative departure from the traditional greenery.

Hang strings of felt balls, dried oranges, yarn tassels, or stars cut from heavy-stock paper as an alternative to traditional pine or cedar garlands. Or, Thomas says, “Mid- to high-tier retailers like CB2 and West Elm use modern shapes and materials to create some very unique and trendy garlands, like one made of crystal shapes and another with gold-frosted palm fronds.”

Metallics are a fun, nontraditional way to set an icy winter scene in your space this holiday scene.

“Metallics can add a sophisticated touch to holiday decor,” says Houston-based interior designer Chandos Dodson Epley of Chandos Collective. “Gold, silver, and bronze create a beautiful shimmer and can be combined with various colors for a modern twist. Pairing metallics with whites and deep greens can really elevate the festive atmosphere.” Plus metallics work well with New Year’s Eve trimmings, for those who like to let their Christmas decorations linger a bit.

You only need a few tasteful figurines to transform an ordinary tabletop into a holiday-themed vignette.

Sticking to one tone for trinkets artfully arranged on a console table or windowsill is a way to add holiday cheer that doesn’t look too busy. Add candles to your window display for an inviting glow that guests can spot as they come up your walkway. For the actual windows, Maggie Griffin of Maggie Griffin Design in Gainesville, Georgia, says nothing tops a traditional wreath. “I love a simple magnolia or boxwood wreath with a long silk ribbon with an understated bow. It’s classic and simple!” she says.

Repurposing leftover upholstery into stocking is a fun, easy DIY project.

If you’ve recently reupholstered, use leftover fabric scraps to create stockings that pair perfectly with your furniture. Or eyeball your existing chairs and couches and try to make a match. The room seen here—with walls painted Aubusson Blue by Annie Sloan—has striped stockings that make even the non-seasonal decor (the chairs) look more cohesive and intentional. Sloan takes the idea a step farther by matching her presents too. The chair, stockings, and gift wrap are all done in Sloan’s Ticking in Olive fabric.

No space for a 9-foot tree indoors? Try decking out a plant.

Designer Bailey Todd of White Cliff Studio in Columbus, Illinois, supports the desire to have multiple Christmas trees, or a decked-out tree and plant combo. “If you have lots of indoor tropical plants in your living room and don’t want to (or can’t) move them, decorate those too,” she says. “Just be sure not to use any heavy decor—keep garlands and ornaments light so you don’t damage any stems.” For a modern spin that’s also ideal for small spaces, skip the evergreen altogether and just go for the potted plant.

No need to completely change the palette of your space just to get it holiday-ready.

Greenfeld is a fan of a beautiful garland draped across the mantel. “When the garland gently hangs over the edges, it creates a soft, organic feel that perfectly frames the mantel and adds elegance without overwhelming the space,” he says. But doing so doesn’t mean you have to ditch your living room’s current, non-holiday color scheme. “I always suggest incorporating colors that complement the room so the garland enhances the space rather than compete with it.”

Subtlety not your thing? Go maximalist this Christmas with a themed tree.

“This year’s holiday decor is all about natural elegance and emotional warmth,” declares designer Anita Yokota, who decked the halls of the White House in 2023. “Real greenery, organic textures, and soft metallics create calm, layered spaces that feel alive.” Here, she’s adorned a tree in more muted, earthy tones alongside ornaments inspired by nature, like mushrooms. Golden accents complement all the browns and tans on the tree, adding just a touch of glamour.

DIY garland making can be a fun holiday activity at home for the whole family.

“I love when holiday decor feels gathered, not purchased,” says Jessica Whitley of Jessica Whitley Studio in Athens, Georgia. “Here, olive and rosemary branches bring sculptural softness to [the mantel’s] dark marble. A few metallic touches, like vintage bells or subtle shimmered ribbon catch the light and make the greenery feel festive without overpowering the space.”

A Christmas village—especially one that doubles as cozy mood lighting—is one way outside of your typical wreaths and trees to lend your home some holiday cheer.

Every surface serves as an opportunity to introduce some festive flair, as seen with this hallway table designed by Renae. Creating a Christmas village is a fun way for little ones to help with DIY Christmas decorations; they can paint buildings (available at craft shops or dollar stores like Dollar Tree) and even mold holiday-themed figurines, like a reindeer and or snowman, from clay. Keeping decor cozy and nostalgic aligns with this year’s trends, according to Renae. “For 2025, I’m all about the cozy, nostalgic vibe of Christmas,” she tells AD. “I love classic plaids, deep reds, and those warm, comforting touches that make any space feel like you’ve stepped into a Christmas movie.”

One simple method of giving your home a dash of holiday happiness? Add a simple runner in red-and-green plaid.

An easy way to weave holiday home decor into unexpected spaces is through rugs. Roll out a mat, runner, or larger carpet for a quick and cozy look. “Seasonal motifs, such as garlands, reindeer, or plaid, instantly make a space feel warm and festive for holiday gatherings,” says Maria O’Brien of Ruggable. Or opt for a yuletide spin on plaid, like a timeless tartan, as seen above. “Heritage-inspired patterns are having a moment, with classic red and green tones adding a touch of tradition to the home,” says O’Brien.

Bells and bows are tried-and-true Christmas classics.

Though model and actor Kara Del Toro lives in Los Angeles, she wanted her home to have a European feel for the holidays. “With our German roots, my mom and grandmother always brought little European touches into our holiday traditions,” she says. “So this year, I wanted to bring that nostalgia and old-world charm into my own home with a quaint European Christmas that complemented its Mediterranean architecture rather than competing with it.” To do so, she sourced cedar, pine, noble fir, olive branches, asparagus fern, red astilbe, and other seasonal flora to make her own garlands. She then added bells and red bows, embellishments you could picture at a Christmas market in Germany.

Pinecones, pomegranates, and oranges add some life to this festive tablescape.

To carrying that old-world feel over to her dining table, Del Toro decided to festoon it with fruit. “I layered all of the greenery with pears, pomegranates, dried orange slices, and pinecones, then added loads of candles for a little sparkle,” she says. “I love how something as simple as fruit or a beautiful branch can feel so festive when you put it all together.”

Exploring alternative options to your traditional Christmas tree? Think outside the box: Most greenery looks merry wrapped in lights and red bows.

If you already have a tree or large plant in your living room, make it the main attraction, like Del Toro did here. “One of my favorite decisions was skipping a traditional Christmas tree altogether,” she says. “I have an 18-foot olive tree named Olivia in my living room, and she’s already the focal point of the space. I thought, why compete with her? Instead, I climbed up on my ladder and dressed her with antique-style bells, twinkling lights, and hand-tied bows. It feels so fitting for a Mediterranean home, and I love that it’s a little unexpected.”

Embroidered napkins can add a festive flair to any holiday party.

If you’re hosting a holiday soirée, an embroidered cocktail napkin—like these, part of a 12 Days of Christmas set from Lettermade—is a small touch that makes a big impact, since your guests will be sitting with and handling them all night. Tying bows around the stems of your glassware is an equally charming detail.

Even if you go big for holiday decor, you don’t have to go against the grain. Tap into your existing color palette and style for Christmas decor if you’re craving a cohesive look.

“When decorating for the holidays, I like to build on the warmth and character of a home by incorporating rich, natural colors like olive, moss and burgundy that complement the existing interiors,” says Jennifer Sissom of Ryan Street Architects in Austin. Here, the team at Ryan Street did just that by mixing in hues that match year-round artwork in jewelry designer Kendra Scott’s Austin home.

Glassy ornaments make for a sleek winter wonderland.

In Scott’s home, the tree is decked with retro-looking mercury glass ornaments. “Looking ahead to holiday trends for 2026, I’m seeing a continued appreciation for vintage and collected pieces, particularly antique ornaments and aged mercury glass, which bring a softness and sense of history to holiday decorating,” says Sissom. “Overall, there’s a shift toward more personal, layered spaces that feel timeless rather than overly seasonal.”

What are 2026’s top trends in Christmas decor?

“This year, the holiday decor trends are grounded in a beautiful balance between nostalgia, whimsy, and sophistication,” says designer Taniya Nayak, a Marshalls and TJ Maxx home style expert. “We're seeing a continued appreciation for timeless holiday pieces, but with more personality, rich textures, and unexpected color combinations. It’s less about following a specific aesthetic and more about creating a home that feels festive, warm, and collected over time.”

While minimalism has had its moment in recent years, Nayak says the trend is shifting toward a more playful, maximalist approach to holiday decorating. “People are embracing more whimsical details like gingham, bells with luxe velvet bows, graphic black-and-white stripes, festive glassware, plaid throw pillows, or an unexpected accent like a faux pearl Christmas tree topper that adds personality and dimension without making the space feel overly styled,” she says. Rich jewel tones—popular last year—are still on trend this holiday season. Deep burgundies, emerald greens, and touches of gold or silver create a glamorous palette.

“I'm also loving food-inspired holiday decor,” says Nayak. “It's fun, fresh, and especially chic when styled in an elevated way.” This might mean glass-frosted ornaments that take the form of plump strawberries or an ice cream sundae. Sardine tins and shrimp have been especially popular when given the glass ornament treatment. Nayak also recommends decorating with citrus, such as tucking dried orange slices into greenery. “You can even bring this trend to your holiday table decor with pears, pomegranates, candles, and beautiful serving pieces,” she says. See Del Toro’s Christmas tablescape above for an example of festive fruit accents.

“My number one rule is that there are no rules when it comes to holiday decorating,” says Nayak. “The holidays are such a special time of joy, happiness, and family, so there’s no shame if you love a head start!” Everyone who has already had their Christmas tree up for a month can breathe a collective sigh of relief. That being said, Nayak also recommends easing into the season and decorating in stages. “You can start introducing cozy textures, scented candles, greenery, and warm lighting in early November. I also personally like to layer in chic serveware and velvet accessories that transition beautifully from Thanksgiving to Christmas. Then, as Thanksgiving approaches or passes, you can bring out more traditional holiday decorations,” she says.

If you're a procrastinator, that’s also perfectly fine.”There’s no deadline for creating a little holiday magic, and you don’t need to splurge or spend weeks decorating to make your home feel magical,” says Nayak.

Whether you’re looking to add small, unique holiday accents, like a beautiful decorative game set, a premium wool blend throw, or a silver-rimmed serving plate that inspires an entire holiday tablescape—or you’re looking to completely overhaul your space into a winter wonderland, it’s nice to have a game plan before you hit the shops.

Sometimes, a few thoughtful additions are all you need to make your home feel festive. As an added bonus, late decorators can also scoop up deals as holiday decor begins to be marked down.

How do I incorporate holiday decorations in more unexpected places throughout the house?

For those truly obsessed with the Christmas holiday, decorations don’t have to be confined to the living room. As shown above, designers have decked out kitchens, bedrooms, and hallways for the season; Button is even bringing the holiday spirit to her bathrooms. “Each year, I choose a new space to gussy up with festive decor,” she says. This year will be the bathrooms as a fun spot. I hide plastic animals with ribbons or mini wreaths on them for my children. It becomes a fun game to discover where the creatures have hidden themselves—sometimes peeking out from the tops of mirrors, or near the towel bar, or by the tub!”

What are some budget-friendly Christmas decor ideas that look expensive?

“Holiday decor doesn’t have to break the bank,” says Nayak. Small touches like festive kitchen accessories, tablescape accents, and natural elements such as garlands and wreaths are affordable ways to channel the holiday spirit. By prioritizing timeless, quality decor, you’ll create a well-curated atmosphere that will last for many seasons to come.

The centerpiece of holiday home decor is usually the tree, so placement is key. Samantha Stathis Lynch, designer and home style expert with Marshalls and TJ Maxx, says, “Christmas trees are often the focal point of holiday decor for those celebrating Christmas, so it’s important to have the tree in a room that is accessible and spacious. The living room or family room is often the most utilized; however, any room in your home can accentuate the tree—it’s all about preference.” Placing your tree in front of a window makes for elegant Christmas decor for your home’s exterior as well. (Is there anything more homey than seeing glowing Christmas lights in a window?) Or place your tree in the living room’s entryway so it can be enjoyed from adjoining rooms and add to your dining room’s ambiance or Christmas kitchen decor.

A cozy Christmas living room is all about texture, Thomas says. “Whether that’s velvet drapes, bouclé throw pillow covers, or a high-pile rug, textiles are the perfect way to add diverse textures to a room without making it feel overwhelming.”

Adding to that, Lynch recommends including subtle lighting, candles, and additional seating around your Christmas tree. “Ottomans or poufs can make any space the perfect area to gather around your tree and celebrate the season,” she says. Temporary seating near a Christmas fireplace is another option. Add throw blankets and trays with hot cocoa mugs to mimic ski chalet vibes. It’ll transform your living room into a cozy spot within a winter wonderland.

How to decorate living room windows for Christmas

Windows are even more real estate for your Christmas theme. “Symmetry across window panes is a largely popular seasonal trend that can be easily achieved with wreaths, candles, or garland,” Lynch says. “Place matching Christmas wreaths within the center of your home’s front-facing windows or candle holders and taper candles within each windowsill for a picturesque holiday home.”

Thomas, on the other hand, prefers more modern Christmas decor, like acrylic nutcrackers or matte white decorative presents. “Gathering these design-forward yet minimal trinkets in groups of three or five to form triangles—or what designers call three-point thinking—provides depth and intrigue to the eye,” he explains. “Windows are essentially built-in frames in a room. Knowing that, any window decor should lead with composition and proportion first, which is why less will always be more when it comes to windows.”

Thomas recommends using Command Clear Hooks for garlands that serve as mantel decor, emphasizing that “these should be in the arsenal of any DIY’er, as they are a great option for temporary solutions.” You could also use a tension rod in a pinch. “I’ve seen some rather creative implementations of this technique where folks will place a tension rod in between a passageway and use that to hang a garland. I will definitely be trying this method this year,” he adds. Before wrapping your garland around the rod, you can even spray-paint it green so it blends in better.

“When it comes to hanging stockings, I’m a traditionalist and I recommend investing in stocking hangers,” Thomas says. “These can be used year after year, and with so many options on the market, one can absolutely find an option that suits the rest of the decor. However, not everyone has real estate like a fireplace mantel to hang stockings, so I recommend some damage-free adhesive hooks.”

#4749. Researchers Just Figured Out a Way to Detect Ovarian Cancer Earlier Than Ever

More than 21,000 women in the U.S. are diagnosed with ovarian cancer each year. While it’s not the most common cancer in women, ovarian cancer is considered the deadliest cancer in women worldwide because it’s often diagnosed at later stages, has a high rate of recurrence, and is difficult to treat. Right now, the five-year survival rate of ovarian cancer is just 52 percent.

As with most cancers, detecting the disease early may increase the odds of survival. Researchers recently discovered a new way to detect earlier stages of the cancer, potentially helping thousands of women. The Nature Medicine study breaks down the mechanisms of a blood-based test that can detect ovarian cancer in its precancerous stages. In theory, this could dramatically impact survival rates in women. The test is still in the research phases, but doctors agree that something like this is needed. Here’s what they want women to know.

Meet the experts: Diana Pearre, MD, gynecologic oncologist at The Roy and Patricia Disney Family Cancer Center at Providence Saint Joseph Medical Center in Burbank, CA; Abdulrahman Sinno, MD, chief of the division of gynecologic oncology with Sylvester Comprehensive Cancer Center, part of the University of Miami Health System

First, some background: Researchers found that women with early-stage high-grade serous ovarian cancer or serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma (STIC), which is a precursor to ovarian cancer, have higher-than-usual levels of a type of RNA called Tu-stroma circulating in their blood.

Tu-Stroma is linked with cancer’s early attacks that weaken healthy cells to make room for cancer cell growth. Spotting Tu-stroma means that doctors have an early molecular warning signal that could suggest cancer is developing before a tumor is detected.

The study itself was conducted on hundreds of women around the world with and without cancer and found that the test detected STIC in 92.3 percent of women with the condition. It also correctly identified 98.2 percent of healthy women. They also tried the test on a high-risk group and found that about 72 percent of positive results were accurate, while negative results were almost 100 percent accurate.

But this is still an early discovery, and the researchers point out in the study that more robust research is needed.

“We have very few ways of detecting ovarian cancer,” says Diana Pearre, MD, gynecologic oncologist at The Roy and Patricia Disney Family Cancer Center at Providence Saint Joseph Medical Center in Burbank, California. “There are no screening tests.” Instead, doctors rely on pelvic ultrasounds and labs to look for tumor markers.

“Unfortunately, we subject women to surgery if and when they have ovarian masses that are suspicious,” Dr. Pearre says. “Having another tool to help us discriminate which tumors are more suspicious would be very helpful in detecting cancers at an early stage.”

Abdulrahman Sinno, MD, chief of the division of gynecologic oncology with Sylvester Comprehensive Cancer Center, part of the University of Miami Health System, agrees. “Eighty percent of high-grade serous carcinoma is diagnosed in advanced stage with no effective screening strategy,” he says.

Previous screening strategies didn’t work because they only spotted cancer at advanced stages, Dr. Sinno says. “Before this, there was no screening test for average-risk women,” he adds.

We’re not at the stage where this can be rolled out to the general public yet. The blood test is still considered experimental and it’s not a clinically validated. Still, doctors say the news is worth following. “This is a promising discovery-stage result, not a test that is ready for prime time,” Dr. Sinno says.

Carina Hsieh, MPH, is the deputy features editor of Women’s Health. She has more than a decade’s worth of experience working in media and has covered everything from beauty, fashion, travel, lifestyle, pets, to health.

She began her career as an intern in the fashion closet at Cosmopolitan where she worked her way up to Senior Sex & Relationships Editor. While covering women’s health there, she discovered her passion for health service journalism and took a break to get her Masters in Public Health. Post-grad school, she worked as a freelance writer and as The Daily Beast’s first Beauty, Health, and Wellness Reporter.

Carina is an alum of the Fashion Institute of Technology and the Yale School of Public Health. She and her French Bulldog, Bao Bao, split their time between Brooklyn and Connecticut. She enjoys reformer Pilates, (slow) running, and smelling the fancy toiletries in boutique fitness class locker rooms.

#4748. This Is How Fast You Should Walk to Help Lower Your Risk of Death

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

New research shows that how fast you walk, whether measured in a clinical test or through daily activity, can help predict your risk of dying from any cause.

The study compared two ways of measuring walking: a short walking speed test conducted in a clinic and the step rate people take in their everyday lives, measured with a wrist-worn device.

Both measures were linked to mortality risk and showed similar ability to predict it.

The findings, published on October 23 in JAMA Network Open, could help doctors and researchers choose the best method for assessing health risks in different settings.

The study was part of the Whitehall II accelerometer substudy in the United Kingdom.

It included 4,067 participants, mostly males, with an average age of about 69 years. About one-third of the subjects were female.

The researchers collected data from January 2012 to December 2013 and followed up through August 2024.

To measure clinical walking speed, participants completed a standard walking test. They walked a marked 2.44-meter course at their usual pace. The test was repeated three times, and the average speed in meters per second was used for analysis. Participants who normally used a cane were allowed to use it during the test.

For free-living walking measurements, participants wore a wrist-worn GENEActiv accelerometer for 9 consecutive days. This device recorded movement at a high frequency and used special software to detect walking episodes and count steps.

From this data, two key measures of walking cadence were calculated: the median walking cadence (the middle value of steps per minute during walking periods) and the 95th-percentile walking cadence (a higher step rate indicating brisk walking). The study also calculated the average number of daily steps.

The researchers additionally gathered information on factors known to affect mortality, such as:

National death records were used to identify deaths during the follow-up period.

Statistical methods were then used to estimate the risk of death associated with walking speed and cadence while accounting for other risk factors.

The models were adjusted step-by-step: starting with no adjustments, then adding sociodemographic factors, behavioral factors, and finally health-related factors.

The ability of walking measures to predict mortality was assessed using a statistical measure.

The study also examined differences between males and females.

The researchers additionally conducted analyses to test how well the results held up when they excluded early deaths, looked at subgroups by age and health status, and used different definitions of walking cadence.

During a median follow-up of nearly 12 years, 739 participants died.

The average clinical walking speed of participants was 1.2 meters per second. The median walking cadence during daily life was about 75 steps per minute, and the 95th percentile walking cadence was about 112 steps per minute.

The study found only a weak correlation between clinical walking speed and free-living walking cadence, meaning the two measures do not strongly reflect the same walking behavior. However, both measures were independently associated with a lower risk of death.

After adjusting for age, sex, lifestyle, and health factors, for every standard increase in clinical walking speed, the risk of death was 23% lower.

Similarly, higher median and 95th-percentile walking cadences were associated with 17% and 18% lower risks of death, respectively.

When examining how well these walking measures predicted mortality, each on its own showed modest predictive ability.

Adding clinical walking speed to a model with other known risk factors slightly improved mortality prediction, while adding free-living walking cadence also improved prediction, albeit to a similar degree to that of clinical walking speed.

Combining clinical walking speed with free-living walking parameters provided a small boost in predictive ability, but the effect was not significant after accounting for detailed health factors.

The study also found that walking speed and cadence had similar predictive power for both men and women, although the overall prediction models performed slightly better for women.

Several sensitivity analyses supported the main findings. Results were consistent when excluding early deaths, focusing on healthier or older participants, and using different ways to define walking cadence.

Overall, this study suggests that clinical walking speed tests and free-living walking cadence measurements from wrist-worn devices are both useful in predicting all-cause mortality risk. They provide similar information but reflect different aspects of walking behavior.

The choice between methods may depend on the purpose of the assessment, available resources, and the context in which the measurement is taken.

Neha Sabharwal, PT, DPT, a physical therapist and director of rehabilitation specializing in geriatric mobility and functional decline at Vintage Faire Nursing and Rehabilitation Center in Modesto, CA, said that walking speed helps predict longevity because it’s an indicator of someone’s overall health.

“Walking is something most of us do without thinking about it, but it requires several body systems to work together,” she told Healthline. “Your heart and lungs have to keep up, your muscles need to produce enough force, and your brain has to coordinate each step while keeping you balanced.”

Sabharwal, who wasn’t involved in the study, said that in her work, she pays attention to when someone starts walking more slowly than before.

“It is easy to dismiss that change as part of getting older, but there may be something else going on,” she said. This could include muscle weakness, pain, reduced endurance, balance problems, or underlying medical conditions.

According to Sabharwal, the current study is valuable because it suggests that useful information about people’s movement can be obtained outside a clinical setting.

However, she cautioned against misinterpreting the findings to mean that simply walking faster will make you live longer.

“People who naturally walk faster may already have better underlying health,” said Sabharwal.

“I would be less concerned about whether someone walks faster than their neighbor and more interested in whether they are walking slower than they did six months ago,” she said.

Theodore Strange, MD, chairman of medicine at Northwell Staten Island University Hospital and senior vice president of the Metro Market Region at Northwell Health, shared some insights for those who may notice their walking speed has declined. Strange wasn’t involved in the study.

“I mean, if it’s slowing down because a week or two ago, you were walking up a flight of steps with no problem, and now, you’re having some shortness of breath, I think it should be evaluated,” he told Healthline.

Strange added that if you’re experiencing aches or pains that weren’t there before, you should consult a healthcare professional, as they can make exercise more difficult.

It’s also essential to manage any chronic diseases that you have so that you can exercise as well as possible within the constraints of your condition, he said.

“And I think slow and steady wins the race here,” said Strange. He suggests monitoring your walking with a device like a pedometer and progressively increasing your steps.

“Everybody talks about 10,000 steps a day. I think the most recent studies show probably 7,000 to 8,000 is adequate,” he said. You can start where you are and work your way up gradually.

Strange further noted that physical therapy can sometimes be helpful if you have issues with gait mechanics, balance, or strength. Additionally, you might benefit from exercise that is tailored to your condition, for example, if you’ve had a stroke.

Finally, Strange advised stretching before and after exercise to keep your muscles moving.

“I go back to adequate nutrition and hydration being important,” he said. You want to make sure you are adequately supporting your body’s ability to exercise, said Strange.
